title: Verbs and their two base forms
goal: Conjugate verbs for six persons, and face the quirk of Estonian that most trips up learners: **every verb has two base forms**.
bekal: conjugate verbs for *ma, sa, ta, me, te, nad*
know when to use the **-ma** form and when the **-da** form
talk about daily activities and hobbies

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Mida sa vabal ajal teed?
dialogs.intro: Evening in the campus library. Budi asks about Kerli's free time.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: What do you do in your free time?

lines.speaker: Kerli:
lines.text: Ma loen palju. Ja ma käin ujumas.
lines.id: I read a lot. And I go swimming.
lines.literal: I read-I much. and I go-I swimming-in.

lines.speaker: Kerli:
lines.text: Mõlemad on olemas, aga eri kohtades.
lines.id: Both exist, but in different places.
lines.literal: both-plural are existing, but different place-plural-in.

lines.speaker: Kerli:
lines.text: Igal tegusõnal on kaks põhivormi: "ujuma" ja "ujuda".
lines.id: Every verb has two base forms: "ujuma" and "ujuda".
lines.literal: every verb-at is two basic-form-part: "swim-ma" and "swim-da".

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: And which one do I use?

lines.speaker: Kerli:
lines.text: See sõltub sõnast enne. "Ma tahan ujuda", aga "ma lähen ujuma".
lines.id: It depends on the word before it. "Ma tahan ujuda", but "ma lähen ujuma".
lines.literal: it depends-it word-of before. "I want-I to-swim", but "I go-I swim-to".

lines.speaker: Kerli:
lines.text: Ausalt öeldes ei tea keegi. Sa õpid selle ära harjumusega.
lines.id: Honestly, nobody knows. You learn it by getting used to it.
lines.literal: honestly saying not knows anyone. you learn-you it-of away habit-with.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: See on nagu inglise keeles "to swim" ja "swimming".
lines.id: It's like "to swim" and "swimming" in English.
lines.literal: it is-it like English language-in "to swim" and "swimming".

lines.speaker: Kerli:
lines.text: Väga hea võrdlus. Peaaegu sama loogika.
lines.id: A very good comparison. Almost the same logic.
lines.literal: very good comparison. almost same logic.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Siis ma tean juba, kuidas mõelda.
lines.id: Then I already know how to think about it.
lines.literal: then I know-I already, how to-think.

lines.speaker: Kerli:
lines.text: Jah. "Ma tahan minna" — nagu "I want to go".
lines.id: Yes. "Ma tahan minna" — like "I want to go".
lines.literal: yes. "I want-I to-go" — like "I want to go".

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ja "ma lähen sööma" — nagu "I'm going to eat".
lines.id: And "ma lähen sööma" — like "I'm going to eat".
lines.literal: and "I go-I eat-to" — like "I'm going to eat".

lines.speaker: Kerli:
lines.text: Just nii. Sa said aru kiiremini kui enamik.
lines.id: Exactly. You understood faster than most people.
lines.literal: exactly so. you got-you understanding faster than most.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Hea. Siis lähme sööma — ma tahan süüa!
lines.id: Good. Then let's go eat — I want to eat!
lines.literal: good. then go-we eat-to — I want-I to-eat!

lines.speaker: Kerli:
lines.id: Ha! Both forms in one sentence.

notes: ⚠️ **Two base forms are a fact to accept, not a rule you can derive.** Estonian dictionaries always list both: *ujuma – ujuda*, *sööma – süüa*, *minema – minna*. Write both in your notebook, just as you wrote noun pairs in unit 6.

**Budi's English comparison is close enough to be useful.** The *-da* form behaves like *to swim* — it follows verbs of will or ability. The *-ma* form behaves like *going swimming* — it follows verbs of motion and starting.
**Käin ujumas** — "I go swimming (regularly)". *Käima* means to go habitually and requires the *-mas* form: *käin tööl*, *käin ujumas*, *käin kinos*. Contrast with *lähen ujuma* (this one time, now).

**Ma loen** from *lugema*. Notice the *g* disappears. Some verbs undergo consonant gradation when conjugated, just like the nouns in unit 6 — and once again the answer is not memorizing rules, but memorizing the *ma* form.

grammars.title: Conjugating verbs — six endings
body: Take the *-ma* form, drop *-ma*, add the ending. For most verbs that is enough.
after: ⚠️ Look at the last two columns: *õppima* loses one *p*, *lugema* loses the *g* entirely. Some verbs undergo gradation — the same pattern as the nouns in unit 6.
**The safe approach:** memorize the **ma** form of every new verb, not the dictionary form. Once you know *ma loen*, the other five forms come out by swapping the ending.
⚠️ The only truly irregular one is *olema*: *olen, oled, **on**, oleme, olete, **on***. The third and sixth rows use the same form, and there is no *-b* or *-vad* at all.

grammars.title: ⚠️ Which form after which verb
body: This is a list you need to own. The good news: both groups make sense once you see the meanings together.
after: **A pattern to hold on to:** verbs expressing **will, ability, permission, and liking** take *-da*. Verbs expressing **motion, beginning, and obligation** take *-ma*.
⚠️ *Tahan* and *pean* side by side show why the rule must be memorized: *ma tahan minna* but *ma pean minema*. Both are "I ... go", yet the forms differ.
If you use the wrong form, Estonians still understand you completely. The mistake marks you as a learner, not as someone unintelligible. Don't let it stop you from speaking.

blocks.text: ⚠️ Notice *minema – minna – ma lähen*. The three forms look like three different words, and this is the verb you will use most often. Learn all three at once, today.

head: Eesti keel
English
rows: What do you do in your free time?
I go to the gym regularly.

blocks.title: ⚠️ Mulle meeldib — the backwards structure
items: Estonian doesn't say "I like books". It says **"to me the book is pleasing"**: *Mulle meeldib raamat.*
As a result, what changes with number is not the person but the **thing**: *Mulle meeldib raamat* (one book), *Mulle meeldi**vad** raamatud* (many books).
*Mulle, sulle, talle, meile, teile, neile* — "to me/you/him-her/us/you all/them". This is the **-le** ending from unit 7, used for people.
When what's liked is an action, use the *-da* form: *Mulle meeldib ujuda.* (I like swimming.)
